items.subject: MA
items.subskill: adding numbers read from a table
items.prompt: The table shows how many cans each class collected for the food drive. How many cans did the three classes collect in all?
items.explanation: Add all three rows: 148 + 265 + 197. Ones: 8 + 5 + 7 = 20, write 0 and carry 2. Tens: 4 + 6 + 9 + 2 = 21, write 1 and carry 2. Hundreds: 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 6. The total is 610.
items.misconceptions: adds only two rows; drops a carried digit

why.A: 410 drops the 2 hundreds carried from the tens column (4 + 6 + 9 + 2 = 21 tens): carry it into the hundreds.
why.B: 413 adds only Room 4 and Room 7 (148 + 265); the question asks for all three classes.
why.C: 590 forgets the 2 tens carried from the ones column (8 + 5 + 7 = 20 ones).

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: difference between the greatest and least value in a table
items.prompt: The table shows the heights of four trees in a park. How much taller is the tallest tree than the shortest tree?
items.explanation: The tallest tree is the Oak, 31 feet, and the shortest is the Pine, 18 feet. 31 − 18 = 13 feet.
items.misconceptions: picks the wrong pair of rows; adds instead of subtracting

why.A: 5 feet compares the tallest tree with the next tallest (31 − 26), not with the shortest.
why.B: 8 feet compares the Elm with the Pine (26 − 18); the tallest tree is the Oak, 31 feet.
why.D: 49 feet adds the two heights (31 + 18); "how much taller" asks for the difference.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: reading a mixed number on a number line
items.prompt: Use the number line to answer the question. What number does point P show?
items.explanation: Between 2 and 3 the line is cut into 4 equal spaces, so each space is 1/4. P is 3 spaces past 2, so P is 2 3/4. Count the spaces, not the tick marks.
items.misconceptions: counts tick marks instead of spaces; counts from the wrong end

why.A: 2 1/4 counts the spaces back from 3 instead of forward from 2: P is three spaces past 2.
why.B: 2 1/3 sees three tick marks between 2 and 3 and calls them thirds; there are four equal spaces, so each is a fourth.
why.D: 3 3/4 has the right fraction on the wrong whole number: P is between 2 and 3, so it is 2 and some fourths.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: distance between two points on a decimal number line
items.prompt: Use the number line to answer the question. What is the distance between point K and point L?
items.explanation: Each small space is 0.1, because 1 to 1.5 is cut into 5 spaces. K is at 1.2 and L is at 1.7. 1.7 − 1.2 = 0.5, which is 5 spaces of one tenth each.
items.misconceptions: counts tick marks instead of spaces; forgets each space is a tenth

why.A: 0.4 counts the tick marks between K and L (there are 4); the distance is the spaces between them, and there are 5.
why.C: 2.9 adds the two numbers (1.2 + 1.7); a distance is how far apart they are, so subtract.
why.D: 5 counts the spaces correctly but forgets that each space is one tenth: 5 tenths is 0.5.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: lines of symmetry of a rectangle
items.prompt: The figure shows a rectangle that is not a square. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
items.explanation: A line of symmetry is a fold where the two halves match exactly. This rectangle folds down the middle and across the middle: 2 lines. Its diagonals do not work, because it is longer than it is wide; only a square has 4.
items.misconceptions: counts the diagonals of a non-square rectangle

why.A: 0: a rectangle folds onto itself both across the middle and down the middle, so it has lines of symmetry.
why.B: 1 finds only one of the two folds; the up-and-down fold and the side-to-side fold both work.
why.D: 4 counts the diagonals too. Fold this rectangle along a diagonal and the corners do not meet: only a square has diagonal lines of symmetry.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: lines of symmetry of an equilateral triangle
items.prompt: The figure shows a triangle with all three sides the same length. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
items.explanation: Fold from any corner to the middle of the side across from it and the halves match. There are 3 corners, so there are 3 lines of symmetry.
items.misconceptions: finds only the vertical fold; counts corners and sides separately

why.A: 1 finds only the fold straight up the middle; because every side is equal, the same fold works from each of the three corners.
why.B: 2 misses one corner: there is a fold from every corner to the middle of the opposite side, and there are three corners.
why.D: 6 counts the 3 corners and the 3 sides as separate folds, but each fold runs from a corner to the middle of the side across from it, so they are the same 3 lines.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: classifying a quadrilateral on a grid
items.prompt: The figure shows quadrilateral WXYZ on a coordinate grid. Which name best describes WXYZ?
items.explanation: The top and bottom are both flat and 4 units long, and the two slanted sides lean the same way (over 1, up 3). Two pairs of parallel sides, with no right angles and not all sides equal, make a parallelogram.
items.misconceptions: calls any slanted four-sided shape a trapezoid or rhombus

why.B: A rectangle has four right angles; the slanted sides here meet the top and bottom at a tilt, not at a square corner.
why.C: A rhombus has four equal sides. The top and bottom are 4 units long, but the slanted sides are shorter, so this is not a rhombus.
why.D: A trapezoid has only one pair of parallel sides. Here both pairs are parallel: the top and bottom run flat, and the two slanted sides lean the same way.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: classifying a quadrilateral on a grid
items.prompt: The figure shows quadrilateral ABCD on a coordinate grid. Which name best describes ABCD?
items.explanation: Only the top (2 units) and the bottom (6 units) are parallel; the two slanted sides lean in toward each other. A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides is a trapezoid.
items.misconceptions: expects slanted sides to mean parallelogram

why.A: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides. The slanted sides here lean toward each other, so only the top and bottom are parallel.
why.B: A rectangle has four right angles; the slanted sides here are not square corners.
why.C: A square has four equal sides and four right angles. The bottom is 6 units and the top is only 2.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: volume by counting cubes
items.prompt: The figure shows a block built from small cubes. Each small cube has edges 1 centimeter long. What is the volume of the block?
items.explanation: The block is 4 cubes long, 2 cubes deep and 3 cubes tall. One layer has 4 × 2 = 8 cubes, and 3 layers make 8 × 3 = 24 cubes, so the volume is 24 cubic centimeters. Count the hidden cubes too.
items.misconceptions: counts only what is visible; adds the edges

why.A: 8 counts only the top layer (4 × 2); there are 3 layers like it.
why.B: 9 adds the edges (4 + 2 + 3); volume multiplies them: 4 × 2 × 3.
why.C: 12 counts only the front face (4 × 3); the block is 2 cubes deep, so there are two such slices.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: cubes needed to complete a larger cube
items.prompt: The figure shows a block built from small cubes. How many more small cubes are needed to make it into a large cube that is 3 cubes long, 3 cubes wide and 3 cubes tall?
items.explanation: The large cube needs 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cubes. The block has 3 × 3 × 2 = 18. 27 − 18 = 9 more — exactly one more layer of 3 × 3.
items.misconceptions: gives the cubes already there; adds only one row

why.A: 3 adds one row of cubes; the missing part is a whole layer, 3 cubes by 3 cubes.
why.C: 18 is the number of cubes already in the block (3 × 3 × 2), not the number still needed.
why.D: 27 is the whole large cube (3 × 3 × 3); take away the 18 already there.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: reading a pictograph with a half symbol
items.prompt: The pictograph shows how many books four students read in March. How many books did Ben read?
items.explanation: Ben has 2 whole symbols and half of one. Each whole symbol is 4 books, so 2 × 4 = 8, and half a symbol is 2 more. 8 + 2 = 10 books.
items.misconceptions: ignores the key; treats a half symbol as 1 or as a whole

why.A: 2 1/2 counts the symbols but does not use the key: each whole symbol stands for 4 books.
why.B: 9 counts the half symbol as 1 book; half of a symbol is half of 4, which is 2.
why.D: 12 rounds the half symbol up to a whole one (3 × 4); a half symbol is only 2 books.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: comparing totals in a pictograph
items.prompt: Use the pictograph of books read in March. How many more books did Ana and Dee read together than Ben and Cole read together?
items.explanation: Ana and Dee: 4 + 5 = 9 symbols = 36 books. Ben and Cole: 2 1/2 + 3 = 5 1/2 symbols = 22 books. 36 − 22 = 14.
items.misconceptions: forgets the key; drops a half symbol

why.A: 3 1/2 is the difference in symbols (9 − 5 1/2); each symbol stands for 4 books.
why.C: 16 leaves out Ben's half symbol: Ben and Cole read 10 + 12 = 22 books, not 20.
why.D: 58 adds all four students; the question compares two pairs, so subtract.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: median from a table
items.prompt: The table shows Ravi's scores on five spelling tests. What is the median of his scores?
items.explanation: Put the scores in order: 78, 84, 88, 91, 95. The middle one of the five is 88, the median.
items.misconceptions: takes the middle row without ordering; finds the mean or range instead

why.A: 17 is the range (95 − 78), how spread out the scores are, not the middle score.
why.B: 78 is the middle row of the table, but the scores must be put in order first.
why.C: 87.2 is the mean (436 ÷ 5); the median is the middle score once they are in order.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: median of an even number of values
items.prompt: The table shows how many minutes Jo read each day for six days. What is the median number of minutes?
items.explanation: In order: 9, 11, 12, 15, 15, 20. With six numbers there are two in the middle, 12 and 15. The median is halfway between them: (12 + 15) ÷ 2 = 13.5.
items.misconceptions: picks one middle value of an even list; confuses median with mode or range

why.A: 11 is the range (20 − 9), not the middle.
why.B: 12 is only the lower of the two middle numbers; with six values the median is halfway between 12 and 15.
why.D: 15 is the mode, the number that appears most often, not the median.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: range from a bar graph
items.prompt: The graph shows how many goals each team scored this season. What is the range of the numbers of goals?
items.explanation: The highest bar is the Bears at 17 and the lowest is the Hawks at 6. Range = 17 − 6 = 11. The Tigers' bar (9) and the Bears' (17) stop between grid lines, so read them carefully.
items.misconceptions: misreads a bar between grid lines; gives the maximum or the total

why.A: 8 subtracts the Tigers (17 − 9), but the lowest bar is the Hawks at 6.
why.C: 17 is the highest bar alone; the range is highest minus lowest.
why.D: 46 adds all four bars; the range is the difference between the highest and the lowest.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: finding two bars with a given total
items.prompt: The graph shows how many students chose each fruit as their favorite. Which two fruits were chosen by 20 students altogether?
items.explanation: Read each bar against the grid lines, which go up by 2: apples 6, bananas 12, grapes 8, pears 10. Bananas and grapes make 12 + 8 = 20.
items.misconceptions: adds the wrong pair of bars

why.A: Apples and pears are 6 + 10 = 16 students, not 20.
why.B: Grapes and pears are 8 + 10 = 18 students, not 20.
why.D: Apples and bananas are 6 + 12 = 18 students, not 20.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: mode from a two-row table
items.prompt: The table shows how many minutes Sam practiced the violin on four days of each week for two weeks. What is the mode of this set of data?
items.explanation: Count each number in both rows: 20 appears 3 times, 15 twice, 25 twice and 30 once. The mode is the number that appears most often: 20.
items.misconceptions: reads only one row; confuses mode with mean or maximum

why.A: 15 appears twice; 20 appears three times, more than any other number.
why.C: 21.25 is the mean (170 ÷ 8); the mode is the number that appears most often.
why.D: 30 is the largest number and appears only once.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: greatest increase on a line graph
items.prompt: The graph shows how many visitors came to a museum each day. Between which two days did the number of visitors increase the most?
items.explanation: Find the change between each pair of days: Mon→Tue +6, Tue→Wed −3, Wed→Thu +9, Thu→Fri −3. The steepest climb is Wednesday to Thursday.
items.misconceptions: picks the highest point instead of the biggest climb

why.A: Monday to Tuesday goes up 6 (12 to 18), but Wednesday to Thursday goes up 9.
why.B: Thursday has the most visitors, but from Thursday to Friday the line goes down.
why.C: From Tuesday to Wednesday the line goes down, from 18 to 15.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: elapsed time from a clock
items.prompt: The clock shows the time a movie began. The movie lasted 1 hour 35 minutes. What time did it end?
items.explanation: The clock shows 3:40: the minute hand is on the 8 and the hour hand has not yet reached the 4. Add 1 hour: 4:40. Add 35 minutes: 4:40 + 20 minutes = 5:00, plus 15 more = 5:15.
items.misconceptions: reads the hour from the number the hour hand is nearest; forgets an hour

why.A: 4:15 adds the 35 minutes but forgets the 1 hour.
why.B: 5:05 subtracts the minutes (40 − 35) instead of adding them.
why.D: 6:15 reads the clock as 4:40 because the hour hand is close to the 4; it has not reached 4 yet, so the movie began at 3:40.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: perimeter of a shape with unlabeled sides
items.prompt: The figure shows the floor of a room, seen from above. Every side meets the next at a right angle. What is the perimeter of the floor?
items.explanation: Find the two unlabeled sides. The top step is 8 − 3 = 5 m across, and the short upright side is 6 − 3 = 3 m. Add all six: 8 + 3 + 5 + 3 + 3 + 6 = 28 m.
items.misconceptions: adds only the labeled sides; finds area instead

why.A: 20 m adds only the four labeled sides; the two unlabeled sides (5 m and 3 m) count too.
why.B: 25 m finds the 5 m side but leaves out the other unlabeled side, which is 6 − 3 = 3 m.
why.D: 33 is the area in square meters (8 × 3 + 3 × 3), not the distance around.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: fraction of a shaded grid
items.prompt: What fraction of the grid is shaded?
items.explanation: 8 of the 20 squares are shaded: 8/20. Divide both by 4 to get 2/5.
items.misconceptions: compares shaded to unshaded instead of to the whole

why.C: 2/3 compares shaded to unshaded (8 to 12); a fraction of the grid compares shaded to all 20 squares.
why.D: 3/2 compares unshaded to shaded (12 to 8), and is more than a whole grid.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: moving a point on a grid
items.prompt: Point K is on the coordinate grid. Kofi moves point K 2 units to the left and 3 units up. What are the new coordinates of point K?
items.explanation: K starts at (5, 3). Left 2 changes the across number: 5 − 2 = 3. Up 3 changes the up number: 3 + 3 = 6. The new point is (3, 6).
items.misconceptions: moves the wrong way; swaps the coordinates

why.A: (2, 5) mixes up the two moves: it goes 3 left and 2 up.
why.C: (6, 3) has the right numbers in the wrong order; the first number is how far across.
why.D: (7, 6) moves 2 to the right; left makes the first number smaller.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: making change from a price table
items.prompt: The table shows prices at the school store. Lena buys 3 pencils and 2 erasers and pays with a $5 bill. How much change should she get?
items.misconceptions: stops at the cost; uses one of each item; regrouping error

why.B: $2.55 is what she spends (3 × $0.45 + 2 × $0.60); the question asks for her change from $5.
why.C: $3.55 subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in each place; $5.00 − $2.55 needs regrouping and is $2.45.
why.D: $3.95 buys only one pencil and one eraser ($1.05); she buys 3 pencils and 2 erasers.

items.subject: MA
items.subskill: reading bars that stop between grid lines
items.prompt: The graph shows how many students signed up for each club. How many students signed up for soccer and art altogether?
items.explanation: The grid lines go by 10, so a bar that stops halfway between two lines is 5 more than the lower one. Soccer is 35 and art is 25. 35 + 25 = 60.
items.misconceptions: rounds a between-lines bar down or up to the nearest grid line

why.A: 50 reads the soccer and art bars down to the grid line below them (30 + 20); each stops halfway to the next line.
why.C: 70 reads both bars up to the grid line above them (40 + 30).
why.D: 95 adds all four clubs; the question asks only for soccer and art.
